blocks.p: I'll clarify what I mean by "mindfulness," since it's a term that gets thrown around a lot. For our purposes, mindfulness refers to an awareness of your present moment experience, whether internal or external. Mindfulness is about being present in the moment and approaching things with curiosity. It's about noticing, watching, and witnessing. Mindfulness doesn't have to be in the woods or on a beach. It doesn't have to be calm and easygoing, and you don't have to be still.

Mindfulness can happen anywhere and at any time, even in a defensive state or while moving around. Of course, some level of safety is required for mindfulness. We don't have the necessary present-moment connection without safety. So, some external environments will be easier than others to be mindful of. And some internal experiences will be easier than others to be mindful of, as well. Your mindfulness ability can grow, but expect limitations.

Unstucking requires mindfulness and meditative practice as its foundation. Mindfulness directs your awareness to the present moment and can lead to anchoring in safety. Meditation builds on mindfulness into an extended, purposeful connection with your internal experience of the present moment.

Mindfulness and meditation are deeply connected. Mindfulness is required for meditation, but meditation is not required for mindfulness. Through these practices, you engage in the actual self-regulation work, the sustained, repeated connection with defensive states while anchored in safety, that builds capacity and creates change.
If you've been [building safety](piece:safety-cues-and-anchors), you've been mindful. But have you been meditative? Not necessarily.
"I've never meditated." That's completely okay. I haven't expected or asked you to. I'll walk you through a general meditation framework and specific skills to build your self-regulation capacity.

"I've tried meditation but don't get it." That's okay, too. Basically, it's a way to connect with your inner world. For our purposes, once you connect, you can then release what's stuck inside. We'll talk more about it later on.
"I hate meditation." That's more of an obstacle, since unstucking relies on meditative practice. Fret not, it can be tolerable.
"I love meditation."
Great! I hope you find a new angle for your meditative practice or a way to deepen your connection with the present moment.
There are questions I always anticipate regarding unstucking:

These questions come up all the time from clients, course students, and the podcast audience. They hear a skill from me and ask some version of these questions. I'm glad they do; it shows they're interested and want concrete next steps. I'm willing to bet you'll ask these questions. You've probably already asked them!
Meditation is a very present-moment-centered practice. It's fluid and welcoming. Yet it's not an intuitive practice. At least not anymore; perhaps it once was.

Because meditation is no longer intuitive, I am forced to break it down and compartmentalize it to teach it, especially in written form. It's not enough to say, "Close your eyes and connect with the present moment." Nope. Instead, I need to explain how to connect with the present moment, why it's important, what to expect, and what to do when things don't go as planned.

What we're left with is a process that is broken down into specific steps that answer these questions. Sometimes those steps are further broken down into smaller steps. This process creates a sequence of skills approach to meditation.

The Skills Sequence is complemented by a deep understanding of what the skills are, how to apply them, why they're helpful, and what to do when things go awry. If I just told you to look inward, you'd probably feel terrified or at least confused. We need to spend a lot of time addressing these top-down questions before addressing the bottom-up experience and allowing self-regulation.

Don't let top-down knowledge intimidate you. As you learn, you'll build confidence and curiosity. As you apply the skills, you'll know what to expect. The top-down efforts will pay dividends for you in the future.

If you base your unstucking practices on this approach, you'll implement a series of skills, one after another. Each skill builds on the last. They may feel clumsy at first, especially if you're new to meditation. As you practice, the skills will flow together more easily. Your cognitive reliance on these learned modules decreases, and they become an innate way of being. You'll know what to expect, and the experience will be less fear-inducing.
But before I teach you what to do, we need to address what not to do.
I know. It's almost sacrilege to say you're meditating wrong. It's a very personal experience, right? It's highly individualized, different from person to person. I totally agree.
And yet I also think you're meditating wrong!
Can we agree on this simple definition of meditation?
Meditation is connecting with your internal experience of the present moment.
Meditation is more than mindfulness of your senses. Meditation brings your conscious awareness to your felt experience of the present moment.

The felt experience of the present moment includes what your senses tell you, yes. But meditation also includes the other felt experiences within you that you typically neglect. These include the body-level sensations of your emotions, such as heaviness when sad or heat when angry. Meditation can also reveal your Polyvagal state's impulses, like collapsing from shutdown or tightening your fists from sympathetic fight activation. Meditation is about anchoring into safety, staying connected to the present moment, and consciously allowing your body's experience.
Perhaps we need to extend our simple definition of meditation with this agreement -
Meditation is connecting with your internal experience of the present moment, whatever it brings.

At least, we can agree that this is an ideal of meditation that you and I will constantly fall short of. As a friend once told me, "The present moment is not always a pleasant moment." Okay, so let's get back to why I think you're meditating incorrectly.

When you meditate, I assume you're rejecting what comes up in the present moment. I assume you reject loneliness or regret when they arise. When you feel the impulse to clench your fists, you tell yourself you shouldn't do so or feel that way. When you feel the heaviness of shutdown, you tell yourself to get over it. This isn't meditation: excuse me, it's not the ideal version of meditation. It's a start! A fantastic start, and we can build from there, no doubt.

I also bet you think meditation means not thinking. Do you think meditation involves "clearing your mind?" This is a common misunderstanding in the meditation world. According to our ideal definition of meditation, "clearing your mind" would be a rejection of what arises cognitively in the present moment. And if you're rejecting an internal experience, that's not really meditation, is it?

"Well, Justin, how can I connect with my internal experiences if my thoughts won't shut up!?" That's a great question. Your thoughts quieting down are a result of connecting to the present moment. Your thoughts aren't the problem. The problem is rejecting your thoughts and trying to control them. When you allow and witness your thoughts, you reduce the friction of fighting them, and they will naturally calm down as a result.

Have you heard the meditative invitation to watch your thoughts as they float through your mind? I like that idea a lot more than stopping your thinking or clearing your mind. But again, watching them float through your mind is a result of connecting to the present moment, not a skill in itself. When you're anchored enough in safety, your thoughts will calm and float on. You'll watch them out of curiosity, without judging or banishing them.

We're thinking beings. Let's not reject that. Allow your brain to have words, images, memories, logic, calculation, and creativity. Yes, even when you meditate. In my deepest meditative experiences, I've found that my cognition is still fully functional… but different. Calmer. More open. More curious. As I lead clients through the upcoming sequential skills, they can still think and talk to me while they deeply explore the inner experience of the present moment. The words don't go away, nor should we try to force them to.

When one meditates, they often do so for a set amount of time, perhaps as a daily ritual. Time is not our concern. It doesn't matter to me whether you meditate for 30 seconds or 30 minutes. The quantity of meditation is unimportant. However, the quality is highly important.

Our meditation goal is to connect honestly with the present moment, whatever it brings. So, if you genuinely connect with your inner world for 30 seconds, you've met the goal. If you sit and try to block your thoughts or feelings for 30 minutes, you have not met the goal.

These skills are sequential. It doesn't matter to me how long it takes you to execute them. If you try for the first time, it will probably take longer, and you may not get very far. If you practice the same sequence of skills each day, you'll get further and further. Some days it will take longer. Some days it will go quicker. And that's okay.

It also doesn't matter to me how many skills you use during a meditation practice. If you try something new, you'll probably only get a couple of steps down the skills sequence. This isn't because you're doing anything wrong. It's perhaps because the skills further down the sequence are just too difficult for you right now.

I prefer that you be honest with yourself about what you can handle. If you can handle only the first couple of skills, embrace them. Focus your efforts on those skills and master them. As you do, the skills further down the sequence become possible.

Let's not worry so much about how meditation should or shouldn't be. Let's focus on what is. Instead of saying, "I should be clear-minded," what if you thought, "My thoughts are scattered"? One statement is a should and a rejection. The other is an acknowledgment of the truth in the present moment.

We don't fight it; we let it be while staying anchored in safety and asking what our felt experience is in the moment. It's far more beneficial to inquire about the internal experience driving scattered thoughts than to try to force clear-mindedness. (As you anchor into and build safety, this way of thinking spontaneously emerges.)

To sum it up, when I say you're meditating wrong, I mean you're trying to make it a certain way. You're rejecting the present moment. You're cutting off internal avenues of connection. You're more focused on the time spent meditating or on using more skills than on the quality of the experience.
"But Justin, aren't you giving us a bunch of shoulds in your sequential skills approach?" you ask skeptically.
No, not really. You can do whatever you want.

I'm going to give you answers to the questions of what, how, and why. I'm not saying you should do it this way or that way. I'm saying the upcoming blueprint is more effective at achieving the idealized version of meditation we agreed on than what you are probably doing, such as rejecting your thoughts and feelings or trying to shut your thoughts up for 30 minutes every morning.

I'm not expecting you to achieve our idealized version of meditation right away. I don't even expect you to sit silently and close your eyes. That may be too much and is very common for someone stuck in a defensive state. The moment they immobilize and close their eyes, they're open to danger. Or when they look inward, they're immediately met with the pains waiting inside.

Realistically, this won't be a home run for you in your first at-bat. You won't get unstuck by doing just one meditative session. Realistically, it'll be challenging. Realistically, it might even be triggering. Realistically, you're going to feel like you're failing. So let's validate all of that right now and normalize it. Heck, we'll even eventually allow those experiences to exist.

Instead of expecting to nail it on the first go (or the second or third), fully expect to try, pause, then try again. You're not failing. The fact that you're learning, attempting, and practicing is a huge win. Huge! Every attempt builds or reinforces a skill, just like practicing anything else.

blocks.why: Thirty honest seconds count. This practice is a few minutes, and stopping early is fine.

blocks.p: You can't hit a baseball without missing a lot of times. As you swing and miss, you'll eventually hit the ball a little, even if it goes behind you or off to the side. As you keep practicing, you'll eventually hit the ball forward, within the field's boundaries. Eventually, you may even hit the ball over the fence for a home run. The same idea applies to drawing a portrait, playing a ukulele, scrambling an egg, and writing a haiku.

No matter what you're learning to do, you'll quickly realize that to get better, you'll need to make minor adjustments to the individual acts. Back to hitting a baseball: it's not enough to just swing. You need to adjust your stance. You need to step forward appropriately and angle your body as you swing the bat. Hitting a baseball isn't a skill. It's the result of an accumulation of much smaller skills, plus practice. And before practicing, you learn.

Unstucking is no different. It's not a skill you use once. It's the result of practicing several smaller skills that you learn first, which will eventually lead to unstucking your defensive state. You're not going to get unstuck in one go, sorry to say. But can you learn something new? Yep, you're doing it right now by reading this. Can you practice one of the upcoming skills? No doubt you can.
As you practice these skills, you're not going to fail. But you might decide to stop or pause. You can [stop and come back](piece:starting-and-stopping) whenever you're ready to.

Do you risk overwhelm? Yeah, you do, in all honesty. But the priority is staying anchored in safety, which should reduce the risk of overwhelm. Even if you do experience overwhelm, that's not a failure. It's an opportunity to learn and make an adjustment to your next intentional practice.

blocks.prompt: How do you feel about meditating? Any thoughts?
What meditation misconceptions did you bring that you're questioning?
